Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:14: And likewise, in the chapter "Acquisition of Torah" (Avot 6), in the Mishnah of Rabbi Meir, who says, "whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake merits many things" etc., he says at the end of his words, "and be modest, slow to anger, and forgiving of insult" — for these things are a preparation for acquiring wisdom. "Modest," as it is written (Proverbs 11:2), "and with the modest is wisdom." "Slow to anger and forgiving of insult," for if he becomes angry his Torah is forgotten, as explained; we say in tractate Sotah (21b): Rabbi Yochanan said, words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Job 28:12), "and wisdom, from where shall it be found?" — thus far his words. And one of the things by which Torah is acquired is patience with a good heart, and it seems to me that regarding this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 14:29), "one slow to anger has great understanding, but one who is short of spirit exalts folly."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:15: Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, peace be upon him, wrote that he heard from Rabbi Meir, the student of Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, that his teacher Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, said to him: the man whose heart moves him to correct his qualities and straighten his ways and deeds, and to pursue humility to the utmost perfection — to be insulted and not insult, to hear his own disgrace and not respond — the Shechinah will immediately rest upon him, and he will not need to learn from flesh and blood, for the spirit of God will teach him. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:16: Further, the aforementioned author wrote elsewhere, these are his words: we found it written in the books of the kabbalists who attained the true path, that one of the great corrections needed by one who seeks knowledge of the LORD is that he be among those insulted, even by his own wife and household, whom he should not fear nor be ashamed before, while he himself should never insult — all the more so with people who are not his household, that he be insulted and not insult. And if he must rebuke members of his household to turn them from the way of death, in which they transgress the will of the Omnipresent, and to straighten and guide them in the way of life, which is the way in which one does the will of the Omnipresent, he should rebuke in such a way that he not become angry in his heart, but his heart should always be joyful, attached to everything. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:17: Likewise, it is written in Tana d'Bei Eliyahu (Zuta, ch. 4), copied in the Yalkut, portion Ki Tisa (§391), these are his words: the Sages taught, be humble toward every person, and toward the members of your household more than toward any person. Further, in Tana d'Bei Eliyahu, portion Atem Nitzavim, on the verse "it is not too wondrous for you" (Deuteronomy 30:11), these are his words: a person should always be humble in Torah and in the fear of Heaven with his father and his mother, his wife, his children, the members of his household, his neighbors, his relatives, and those distant from him, even with a gentile in the marketplace, so that he be beloved above and cherished below and accepted by the creatures, and fill his days and years with a good name; and through this his wife and household will fear him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:10), "and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the LORD is called upon you, and they shall fear you." Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose. And without doubt, whoever trains himself to be insulted by his household and not insult will be humble toward all and will acquire in his heart the attribute of humility — for if he is insulted and does not insult within his own house, where they are subjugated under his hand, all the more so with others.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:18: Further, among the category of the merit of humility is what is said in Kiddushin (71a), that the Name is transmitted only to one who is in the middle of his years and does not become angry. And I heard a story about the pious Rabbi Yaakov Ashkenazi, of blessed memory, who was a wondrously wise man and wanted to teach his wisdom to Rabbi Yehoshua the Pious; but first he tested him regarding anger, for they had a tradition not to transmit the wisdom except to one who, when tested with anger, would not become angry — and he tested him six times, and he bore it, but on the seventh he did not stand firm, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:19: The tenth merit, which is the cause of all the merits mentioned, is that the Shechinah rests with the humble and the lowly, as is explained in Sotah (5a), which we copied above (ch. 1), while the Shechinah flees from the proud and the angry, as explained above (ch. 2).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:20: This is further explained in the Mechilta (portion Yitro), these are his words: "and Moses drew near to the thick darkness" (Exodus 20:18) — what caused this to him? His humility, as it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" — and his end was to cause the Shechinah to rest with man on earth, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "thus says the High and Exalted One, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy: I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the crushed and humble of spirit," and it says (ibid. 61:1), "the spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble, He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted," and it says (ibid. 66:2), "and all these My hand has made... but to this one I look — to the poor and contrite in spirit," "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalms 51:19).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:21: And whoever is proud of heart causes the land to become defiled and the Shechinah to depart, as it is said (ibid. 101:5), "the haughty-eyed and proud of heart, him I cannot [endure]," and every proud heart is called an abomination, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart," and idolatry is called an abomination, as it is said (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and do not bring an abomination into your house" — just as idolatry defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart, so whoever is proud of heart defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart. Thus far his words. And I have heard in the name of the Midrash a proof that the proud are hated before Him, blessed be He, from His command (Leviticus 2:11), "for no leaven nor any honey shall you burn [as an offering]" — the reason being that honey boils in fire and produces froth, and likewise leaven boils and rises, and this alludes to the proud; therefore no fire-offering to the LORD shall be made from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:22: We find, then, that pride and anger resemble one another in this punishment — for just as the angry person defiles himself, being as though he were idolatry, as explained, so he also causes the Shechinah to depart, like the angry person.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:23: Now that a person considers all the merits that belong to one who is humble, lowly, and overlooks his own way, as we have explained, he should see with the eye of his intellect that it is far more fitting for him to suffer a small distress for a great reward, rather than lose in a single moment all the merits mentioned, and come to cause great loss — that his soul and the Shechinah depart from him — and how much toil is needed until the impure spirit within him departs, as explained in the Zohar, saying "would that he be sanctified," and saying "and once it has fled from him once, how much must the person do until it returns to its place" — thus the sinner loses much good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:24: This is like a parable of a person who holds in his hand a cup of water and a jug of balsam oil, and some trouble befalls him, and he must necessarily release one of them from his hand, letting it be lost — surely the way of intellect is that he should suffer a small loss, the cup of water, in order to gain a great profit, the balsam in his hand; and if he does the opposite, he is certainly a fool. In exactly this manner is the matter of anger: if a person suffers by not responding to his own disgrace, and forgoes the honor of his own body, which is a small loss — indeed no loss at all in the eye of intellect — he gains a great profit for the merit of his soul, that his transgressions be overlooked, as we have elaborated regarding the other merits mentioned.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:25: Further, another way to avoid coming to anger is to think that the sufferings through which sins are atoned are of two different kinds: either accepting sufferings upon oneself through fasts, sackcloth, and ashes, as King David, peace be upon him, did, or through the death of children, which is an altar of atonement, as is known; and likewise death itself atones for everything, even desecration of the Name, when repentance has preceded it, as explained in the divisions of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael used to expound (Yoma 86a). Now, all these are hard for a person to bear, and very bitter, especially the death of children or one's own death; and behold, a person mortifies himself with mortifications for the atonement of his sins, and sometimes these involve neglect of Torah and neglect of prayer — how much more pleasant would it be for him to accept light sufferings that do not involve neglect of Torah and prayer, and accept them with love for the atonement of his sins, and rejoice when they disgrace and shame him, knowing that the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him by sending him such light sufferings to purify his sins. And let him who disgraces him bear his own sin, for he is an evil strap [used] to strike this one, as it is said (Isaiah 10:5), "woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:26: It is fitting that he pray to the Holy One, blessed be He, in all his prayers — morning, afternoon, and evening — that the Holy One, blessed be He, grant him the merit of the attribute of humility and submission, and that he be joyful in these sufferings if they disgrace and anger him, and all the other attributes of humility written in this gate, and pray for all of them; and through this he will be reconciled to the Holy One, blessed be He, and be atoned for what he has sinned until now through anger and pride — and since this is his request, he will not become angry nor respond to the one who disgraces him. These two ways of acquiring humility I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:27: I have also heard that it is impossible for a person to attain the merit of holiness and repentance until he has properly acquired in his heart the attribute of humility, and removed from himself the attribute of anger entirely — for one of the twenty-four things that delay repentance is being a man of wrath. Furthermore, he may toil greatly to attain the acquisition of holiness, but when he becomes angry for a moment, it all departs, and we find that all his toil was in vain and wasted his entire life; and when he returns in repentance, he will toil greatly until he is sanctified, and would that he be sanctified — but if he returns and becomes angry, he has lost all he did and toiled in vain, as explained, and there is no end to the matter until he acquires the attribute of humility in its completeness, with the conditions that will be explained regarding it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:28: Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (ch. 6) that the Sages, when they entered into repentance, would swear a solemn oath not to become angry, and he elaborated on this at length. I say that the oath should be not to become angry except regarding a matter the Torah has permitted anger over, such as against the wicked, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD, and loathe those who rise against You?" and likewise to be angry at a student, as is said (Ketubot 103b), "cast bile among the students"; and if he becomes angry over other matters, he should impose upon himself a known penalty by which he suffers, and not annul his oath, in order to fulfill what is said (Psalms 15:4), "he swears to his own detriment and does not retract." And he should conduct himself this way for a year or two, until he has acquired the attribute of humility.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:29: I further say that it is good for a person to make himself a short memorandum on the punishments for anger and pride, and the merits of humility, and read them every day — this device is also sound, for who is the fool who would wish to lose a great loss for a small gain? It is only that at the time of anger he forgets all the punishments and all the merits he will lose; and when he persists in reading, the study will bring him to practice, and he will be diligent and careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:30: I say further that it is possible to reinforce this second aspect with the statement of our Sages of blessed memory in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah, ch. 34) on the verse (Exodus 25:10), "and they shall make an ark of acacia wood": these are their words: Elihu came and said (Job 37:23), "Shaddai — we cannot find Him, He is exalted in power" — whoever hears this verse might say, is this perhaps blasphemy, God forbid? Rather, this is what Elihu said: we do not find the might of the power of the Holy One, blessed be He, exercised in a burdensome way with His creatures, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come upon His creatures with burdens — He does not come upon a person except according to his own strength. You find that when the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the Torah to Israel, had He come upon them with the full force of His power, they could not have withstood it, as it is said (Deuteronomy 5:22), "if we continue to hear" etc. — rather, He came upon them only according to their own strength, as it is said (Psalms 29:4), "the voice of the LORD is with power" — it does not say "with His power" but "with power" — the power of each and every individual. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:31: From this statement the rebuke I wrote in the name of my teacher, peace be upon him, is understood: for if they say to a person, why did you not perform mortifications and fasts, he may say that he did not have the strength for it, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come upon His creatures with burdens; but if they say to him, why did you become angry and cast off from yourself the awe of Heaven, what will he answer his Creator? Surely his evil inclination must be overcome, and it is within a person's power to overcome it without any mortification at all — he need only take it to heart and accept upon himself not to be irritable and to overlook his own way, for (Psalms 10:12 [context of trust]) what does the LORD your God ask of you? For awe is with you so fully that you need not seek after it through a loss of money or similar things external to you.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:32: Further, there is support for my teacher's rebukes in the verses of the Prophets and the Writings: first, what the prophet wrote (Zephaniah 2:3), "seek righteousness, seek humility." Further, what he said (Lamentations 3:30), "let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with disgrace; let him put his mouth in the dust."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:33: Further, he should think of what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 15:4), "in whose eyes a vile person is despised." It is known that if a person is despicable in his own eyes and thinks himself despised, he will not respond to his own disgrace. "Despised" — he should think of the lowness and worthlessness of his soul, that he is despised in the eyes of the Creator because of his evil deeds; further, he should think of his own worthlessness in his life and in his death — in life, from the worm and lice on his head, as our Sages of blessed memory explained (cf. Kohelet Rabbah 5:12), "how much less man, who is a worm [rimah]" (Job 25:6) — these are the lice on his head; and in his death, "and a son of man, a maggot [tola'ah]" (ibid.) — that he is despised because of the decay and foul odor within his innards, as they explained, that at the time a person enters the privy they say to him, see your end. When he considers this, he certainly will not respond to his own disgrace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:34: For this intent the Tanna said (Avot 4:4), Rabbi Levitas of Yavneh says, be exceedingly, exceedingly humble of spirit, for the hope of man is the worm. Many interpretations have been given for this Mishnah, and what seems to me [correct] in his saying "the hope of man is the worm" is this: since we hold that anything that is destined to be done is considered as though already done, then since man's hope [i.e., his destiny] is to become entirely worm, he should think that already, while still alive, he is partly worm — the proof being the lice on his head, as our Sages of blessed memory explained in the Midrash, "how much less man, who is a worm" — these are the lice on his head; and once he thinks this, he will be lowly in his own soul's eyes, for if he considers himself, when disgraced, as already dead and full of worm, he will pay no heed to what people say, thinking in his heart and saying, would a dead man, full of worm, respond to his own disgrace? Certainly he would not respond, for that would be beyond reason.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:35: Further, my teacher wrote another path to acquiring humility: that he should always strive to flee from honor, and choose the lowliest of places, and likewise strive to honor all creatures, poor and rich alike, as equals — for there is no difference between the rich and the poor except in money, but both were created in the image and likeness [of God], and whoever honors the creatures honors the Supernal Craftsman who made them in His likeness, and if, God forbid, he disgraces them, he is as one who disgraces the craftsman who made them — along the lines of what they said in tractate Ta'anit (20b) about Rabbi Elazar, who encountered a very ugly man, etc., and said to him, go to the craftsman who made me and tell him how ugly is this vessel You have made — until he had to ask him for forgiveness, and he [the ugly man] said to him, I forgive you. Further, he should always think of his own disgrace and lack of knowledge, and the loathsomeness of his own decay, and that he is worm and maggot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:36: Further, I heard from him that when he is disgraced and shamed, he should think that Samael stands and accuses him above, and this is a strap drawn from him — for it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him." Therefore King David, peace be upon him, for the atonement of his sin, was silent when Shimi ben Gera disgraced him, calling him "a man of blood" (2 Samuel 16:7), "an adulterer, illegitimate, wicked, oppressor, abomination," as Rashi, of blessed memory, explains on "and he cursed me with a grievous curse [kelalah nimretzet]" (1 Kings 2:8) — an acronym as explained — for David knew that Shimi was a messenger from above, to strike him with his tongue, and in his deed of throwing dust, etc. (2 Samuel 16:13), and he said that the LORD had told him to curse David, and who is to say why he did so? Therefore he worried about his sins and did not respond to his own disgrace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:37: Along these lines the pious author wrote in Chovot HaLevavot, Gate 5 (Gate of Unity of Action, ch. 5), that this is the meaning of (Avot 3:10), "anyone with whom the spirit of the creatures is pleased, the spirit of the Omnipresent is pleased with him" — for whoever is good in His eyes, blessed be He, the Holy One, blessed be He, sows His love in the eyes of the creatures, that they love him; therefore, if they disgrace him, it is fitting that he be silent, for certainly the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him, and he should worry about his sins.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:38: Further, he should think that everything the one who disgraces him says is true, for he does not say even one part in a thousand of his sins, as the liturgical poet wrote, "my sins, were my neighbors to complain of them, they would have fled and distanced themselves from my borders." And even though they harm him, their harm does not reach the level of what he himself has blemished above — for no man has ever taken his fellow's bed from beneath him, as he himself has done, being a slanderer who separates a close friend [from God]; how can he ignore the great war Samael wages against him over his sins, and become absorbed in the small war [of this insult]? Thus far I have heard.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:39: I offer a great rebuke for the acquisition of humility, and for not responding to one's own disgrace and not becoming angry: it is like a parable of a man who went to the king and pleaded and prostrated himself before him, that he come to dwell with him, and the king, out of his great humility, agreed to dwell with him in his house. As the days passed, this man did disgraceful things before the king until the king fled from him. Surely such a man deserves reproach, and we would say he is far from human decency, for by doing those things before the king he thereby drives the king out of his house by force — for a king does not tolerate having a chamber-pot brought before him until he flees, or having a servant crowned in his place and the king expelled — and yet he had pleaded that the king come dwell with him!
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:40: The parallel is understood: we, the people of Israel, all our prayers, mitzvot, and Torah are meant to draw the Shechinah to dwell with us, as it is said (Exodus 25:8), "and let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" — literally among them, within their hearts. This premise is explained in the Zohar and Tikkunim and in several places, that Israel construct a form [for the divine indwelling]; and likewise in the Zohar (portion Terumah, 133a), that whoever prepares for the Holy One, blessed be He, a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand — the Holy One, blessed be He, will be his guest every day, and the matter is explained there in the secret of prayer; see there. And it is known that the King's dwelling is a broken and crushed heart, as we have explained, and its opposite is anger and pride.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:41: We find, then, that the angry person crowns the servant who denies the foundation [of faith], and expels the Shechinah that was dwelling in the soul within his heart; therefore the soul departs, and likewise the Shechinah, as explained. Therefore the Shechinah will certainly not dwell with a person who casts her from her place and expels her whenever he wishes — unless the Shechinah knows for certain that he has already accepted upon himself not to become angry again, and only then will she return to dwell with him. This is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in the statement from portion Tetzaveh (182a) that we copied above: "unless the person comes and uproots it entirely and forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon it" — this being the drawing back of the holiness of his soul that had departed from him, and likewise the drawing back of the Shechinah, for the dwelling of the Shechinah is in the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:42: For the reason of this parable, together with the statement of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Zohar, portion Beshalach, 55b), which we copied in the Gate of Love, chapter 6, regarding "your friend and your father's friend" — see there. This parable is likewise a moral lesson regarding all the sins by which a person sins against the Shechinah, for he certainly expels her from himself, since all transgressions are the stench of the kelipah, and a king tolerates only the good scent of Torah and mitzvot. This is what is said there on the verse (Proverbs 25:17), "withhold your foot from your neighbor's house" — withhold your inclination so that it not boil up against you and rule over you, etc., as explained there — that with every deed of the evil inclination that he lets rule over him, he drives away the holy soul and the Shechinah from himself, and this is not fitting, since He [the Shechinah] is "your friend and your father's friend," as explained there, that He wishes to dwell with you — so do not do deeds that will drive Him from your house.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:43: For another reason as well, it is fitting not to become angry, since one thereby nullifies the commandment to fear the glorious and awesome Name (Deuteronomy 28:58) — for one who stands before the king and fears him does not become angry before him, but is ashamed and fearful of him and leaves all his affairs to the king, since it is in his power to correct everything; and perhaps that one who disgraces him is acting with the king's permission, as King David, peace be upon him, said (2 Samuel 16:10), "the LORD has told him to curse." And so Shmuel said in Nedarim (22b), in the statement we copied above in the preceding chapter: whoever becomes angry, even the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him — not to mention his own soul, hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory, whom the angels honor, and his fellow, made in the image and likeness, whom he must honor, for "who is honored? He who honors the creatures" — but even the Shechinah, whose glory fills the whole earth, and whom he must fear — this is (Psalms 10:4), "God is not in any of his schemes" — meaning "any" [kol] — not a single one of his thoughts is toward the Name, and "kol" is like the phrase "you shall do no manner of work" (Exodus 20:10), and there are many similar cases. Through this is explained what is explained in the Zohar (portion Naso, 145a), that whoever has awe has humility and piety; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:44: When a person takes to heart that all the causes that befall him all come from Him, blessed be He, for He watches over every detail — for they said (Chullin 7b), a person does not so much as strike his finger below unless it is proclaimed above — he will not become angry at the deed of the LORD. And regarding something like this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 16:3), "commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:45: For another reason as well, it is fitting not to respond to one who disgraces him — the warning of King Solomon, peace be upon him (Proverbs 26:4), "do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also become like him." One must be precise about the doubling in his words, saying "a fool according to his folly." Also, the words "also... yourself" are superfluous, since he already said "lest you become like him." It is possible to say that the verse gives three reasons not to respond to a fool. The first is precise in saying "according to his folly" — the meaning being that since he is a fool, the kelipah, which is his folly, has clothed itself in him to say those things, and he resembles a barking dog which one need not worry about. The second reason: "lest you become like him" — for since his words had an effect within his [the responder's] heart, causing him to depart from holiness and words of Torah, the kelipah has also entered his own heart, since out of anger he answered him; thus he becomes exactly like the fool — for the fool who became angry and answered folly certainly [reacted because] they did something to him worth being upset about, and his response is called his "folly"; likewise the wise man who responds to him because his words made an impression on him is just like him, for it is fitting that a man wise in the wisdom of Torah not let vain words make an impression on his heart, even if it were a disgrace to him — the proof of this being Moses our teacher, peace be upon him: when Aaron and Miriam spoke against him, it is written there (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" — the commentators explained that he heard and was silent and did not take it to heart to respond, the reason being that from the greatness of his attachment to the Name he paid no heed to respond to worldly words, and the Name answered on his behalf. And third, "also yourself [gam atah]" — meaning, the soul that is with you — this is alluded to in the word "atah" [you], for the essential person called "atah" is the soul, since the body is finished, lost, and has no permanence to be called "atah"; and when a person speaks with his fellow, he does not speak with his body but with his soul, which sees and hears. And the doubling ["also... yourself"] alludes to the fact that the Shechinah also departs, as explained in the statement we copied from portion Tetzaveh, that the angry person's soul and the Shechinah depart from him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:46: The pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz wrote regarding the Mishnah (Avot 4:4), "be exceedingly, exceedingly humble of spirit" — fitting words for this discourse, which I saw fit to copy here. He raised a difficulty: the Tanna should have said "your hope is the worm," since he began in the second person, saying "be [humble]." And he answered, of blessed memory, saying that pride is of two kinds, and correspondingly there are two kinds of lowliness. The first: one who is proud and thinks that honor befits him, that all should honor him, while he himself does not honor others, like the king and the officials. The correct measure regarding this is that he honor every person according to his level, and think that he and they were created for His honor, blessed be He, and it is not fitting to make use of His creatures, made in His image and likeness, [for one's own glorification] — and this is the attribute mentioned above. Regarding this kind of pride our Sages of blessed memory said (cf. Sotah 5a): the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Pride, "you and I cannot dwell in the same place" — the reason being, as I have written, that honor befits Him, blessed be He, alone, since there is none above Him, and this is what is said (Psalms 93:1), "the LORD reigns, He is clothed in majesty."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:47: The second [kind]: one who disgraces, insults, and berates people, considering them as nothing and void; regarding this he warned, "do not disgrace any person." The correct measure is to be silent and not respond to one's own disgrace, and for this he must be very lowly in his own eyes, like mere dust, so as not to feel it at all. This is why the Tanna said, "be exceedingly, exceedingly humble of spirit" — if others disgrace you, do not be afraid of them and their disgraces — and he gave the reason, "for the hope of man" — for that arrogant man who disgraced and berated you, tomorrow the worm shall consume him, so what is he to you and his disgrace? And this is the reason he said "enosh" [man, in the sense of frail mortal] and did not say "adam," which would have been more fitting since man was taken from earth [adamah] — but he intended what we have written, to admonish the one who is insulted.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:48: Consider, reader, this interpretation, for it is consistent from every side, and this interpretation was pointed out to me by Isaiah, peace be upon him, when he said (Isaiah 51:7), "listen to Me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My Torah — fear not the disgrace of man [enosh], and be not dismayed at their reviling, for the moth shall eat them like a garment, and the worm shall eat them like wool, but My salvation shall be forever, and My righteousness for all generations." Behold, the Tanna cited the language the prophet used, "the hope of man is the worm," but the prophet first said, "listen to Me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My Torah" — for people of this high level are few. For among the first kind [of humility, regarding pride] you will find many people who honor each person according to his level, but that one hears his own disgrace and remains silent — there is not even one; and one who does so shows that he is mostly attached to the supernal world, "with the angels whose dwelling is not with flesh," and therefore does not feel the disgrace of the world. Therefore King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 14:29), "one slow to anger has great understanding," [and] "every man" etc. (Proverbs 19:11) — and I have explained the Mishnah "who is honored" with Heaven's help elsewhere.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:49: So that my words enter your ears, I shall give you a parable of a man who had two pearls, one beyond price, worth thousands upon thousands of gold coins, and the other worth a thousand gold coins; and they robbed him of the second one — could that man possibly grieve when the first pearl, which lacks nothing, still remains? So too, people whose souls are very holy and who have merited to see their own world during their lifetime do not concern themselves with the loss of the good things of this world; all of it is like the peel of garlic in their eyes — at its abundance they do not rejoice, and at its lack they do not worry.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:50: My masters and my geniuses, look and see: the supernal holy one Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, for whose sake the whole world was sustained, was content with a kav of carobs from Sabbath eve to Sabbath eve (Berachot 17b); and Elijah, peace be upon him, "a girdle of leather about his loins" (2 Kings 1:8), and his meal was a cake baked on coals and a jug of water (1 Kings 19:6) — this is nothing but the strength of their faith in their Creator and the intensity of their attachment and cleaving to Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:51: Therefore the prophet said, "those who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My Torah," for this attribute is found only in one whose 248 organs and 365 sinews desire Torah, which grows in his heart this supernal attribute of which they said (Avodah Zarah 20b), "humility is greater than all of them," and it is this that brings one to the holy spirit, as it says (Isaiah 61:1), "the spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble, He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted" — and these are the ones who rise to this great and wondrous level. This is the conclusion of the prophet's words, peace be upon him: "but My salvation shall be forever, and My righteousness for all generations," for God, blessed be He, is destined to raise the horn of the insulted, who hear their own disgrace and do not respond.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:52: Know that the clear proof regarding a person is whether the Name is continually before him, for this is the fruit of the whole Torah, as it says (Deuteronomy 10:20), "you shall fear the LORD your God, serve Him, and cling to Him" — [the fruit being] lowliness, and its opposite, pride. I shall give you a parable of this: two men, each with a thousand dinars — one is in a village where none of its inhabitants attain a thousand gold dinars, and he undoubtedly becomes proud over the villagers; the other dwells in Tyre, whose merchants are princes — this one considers his wealth lowly in his own eyes and as nothing. So too, one who is far from the Name, blessed be He, and from His angels and His pious ones, becomes proud over those beneath him; but the righteous, who have the Name continually before them, lower themselves before Him to the dust, for by looking at the greatness of the Name, His angels, and His pious ones of old, they become very lowly in their own eyes — and one of the eleven general principles of the Torah is "in whose eyes a vile person is despised" (Psalms 15:4).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:53: See Solomon's testimony, peace be upon him (Proverbs 15:28), regarding all we have said: "the heart of the righteous meditates to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things; the LORD is far from the wicked, but He hears the prayer of the righteous." This means that the righteous man's heart continually meditates on what will draw from it humility and lowliness; but the wicked are not content that their hearts are proud, but must also express their pride with their mouths, so that they continually pour out evil things. And the reason for this is that the LORD is far from the wicked and they do not meditate on Him, whereas the righteous — the LORD hears their prayer, since they are continually holy [devoted] to Him.
